      • 14. Permutations and symmetry groups

      14. Permutations and symmetry groups#

      Suppose we paint each corner of a square black or white. There are ways to do this. If the square is a tile that can be picked up and turned, a painting and the same painting rotated by a quarter turn look identical, and we may want to count paintings that look different. Before we can count anything of this kind, we need a precise description of the motions that move the square onto itself and of how two such motions combine. This note describes each motion by the way it rearranges the corners, that is, as a permutation. Collections of permutations that are closed under combining and undoing, called groups, are the setting for the counting methods of the rest of this unit.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Describe a rotation or reflection of a square or a regular polygon as a permutation of its corners.

      • Compose and invert permutations, keeping track of the order in which they are applied.

      • Write a permutation in cycle notation and count its cycles.

      • Decide whether a set of permutations is a group, and count the symmetries of a regular polygon.

      • Compute the order of a permutation from its cycle lengths.

      14.1 Symmetries of a square#

      We label the corners of a square counterclockwise, starting at the bottom left, as in Figure 1. A rigid motion of the plane (a rotation or a reflection) that carries the square onto itself sends corners to corners, so it rearranges the labels. For example, the counterclockwise rotation by about the center, which we call , moves corner to the position of corner , corner to the position of corner , corner to the position of corner , and corner to the position of corner . We record this as

      A rigid motion keeps distances unchanged. Two corners of the square are adjacent if they are joined by a side; adjacent corners are at distance equal to the side length, and the two non-adjacent pairs, and , are farther apart. A rigid motion carrying the square onto itself therefore sends adjacent corners to adjacent corners. We use this property as our definition.

      Definition 1 (Symmetry of the square)#

      A symmetry of the square is a rearrangement of the corner labels such that whenever corners and are adjacent, the corners and are also adjacent.

      Of the rearrangements of the labels, only a few satisfy this condition, and we can count them with the product rule.

      Proposition 2 (The square has eight symmetries)#

      There are exactly symmetries of the square.

      Step 3: Every such choice is a symmetry.

      The four choices of and two choices of give rearrangements. In each of them, and are the two corners adjacent to , and is the corner opposite , which is adjacent to both and . So each rearrangement sends the four adjacent pairs to adjacent pairs, and it is a symmetry. By the product rule there are exactly symmetries.

      Most rearrangements of the four labels are not symmetries. There are rearrangements, and only of them are symmetries. For example, the rearrangement that exchanges and and leaves and in place sends the adjacent corners and to and , which are not adjacent.

      14.2 Permutations and composition#

      14.2.1 Permutations#

      A rearrangement of labels is a function that sends each label to a label and uses every label exactly once.

      Performing one symmetry of the square and then another moves the square onto itself again. In terms of labels, we apply one function and then the other.

      14.4 Groups of permutations#

      14.4.1 Definition and first examples#

      The eight symmetries of the square have three properties. The identity is a symmetry. The composition of two symmetries is a symmetry: if and both send adjacent corners to adjacent corners, then so does . The inverse of a symmetry is a symmetry: a symmetry sends the four adjacent pairs to four different adjacent pairs, so it sends the set of adjacent pairs onto itself; therefore every adjacent pair is for some adjacent pair , and sends it back to the adjacent pair .

      Definition 11 (Group of permutations)#

      Let be a finite set. A group of permutations of is a set of permutations of such that

      1. the identity belongs to ;

      2. if and , then ;

      3. if , then .

      The number of elements is called the order of .

      In this unit, group always means a group of permutations of a finite set. In more advanced courses, groups are defined by rules for an abstract operation; every finite group in that sense can be described as a group of permutations, so we lose no examples by working with permutations.

      The square and the full set of permutations give the first examples, and smaller groups sit inside them.

      • The four rotations form a group: a rotation followed by a rotation is a rotation, and the inverse of a rotation is a rotation.

      • is a group of order .

      14.4.3 Symmetries of regular polygons#

      The same construction works for a regular polygon with corners. We label the corners counterclockwise. Corners and are adjacent for , and corners and are adjacent. A symmetry of the regular -gon is a permutation of that sends adjacent corners to adjacent corners, and the symmetries form a group , the dihedral group. The rotation by counterclockwise is the cycle , and its powers form the rotation group .

      The count of symmetries of the square extends to the -gon.

      Proposition 14 (Order of the dihedral group)#

      For , the regular -gon has exactly symmetries. Exactly of them are rotations.

      Proof#

      The argument of Proposition 2 applies with corners. A symmetry is determined by , with choices, and , which must be one of the corners adjacent to . Once and are known, must be the corner adjacent to other than , then must be the corner adjacent to other than , and so on around the polygon. Conversely, each of the choices places consecutively around the polygon, counterclockwise or clockwise, and so gives a symmetry. By the product rule there are symmetries.

      The rotation , for , moves every corner steps counterclockwise. These rotations have different values , and in each of them is the next corner counterclockwise after . So the rotations are exactly the symmetries that place the corners counterclockwise.

      The other symmetries place the corners in clockwise order. Moving from to moves from to , one step clockwise, so places the corners consecutively in clockwise order, and it is a symmetry. The permutations have different values at corner , so they are exactly the clockwise symmetries.
